  "headline": "Intake maps S1-S2 to a greenfield, local-only, server-authoritative Battleship game with Node tests; 8 key questions recorded, none needs a person, and the result is playable locally only after the final return.",
  "outcome": "done",
  "questions": [
    {
      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds",
      "category": "requirements",
      "changes": "Game engine rules, grid and fleet constants, win detection, the test fixtures, and the UI layout.",
      "default": "Classic Hasbro rules. The board is 10x10 (A-J by 1-10). The fleet is Carrier 5, Battleship 4, Cruiser 3, Submarine 3, Destroyer 2. Ships may touch but not overlap and are straight lines only. Turns alternate with one shot each, whether or not it hits. The player shoots first. Sinking a ship is announced by name. The first side to sink all five ships wins. This rules out salvo variants, other board sizes, special weapons and custom fleets.",
      "id": "Q1",
      "question": "Which Battleship ruleset applies: board size, fleet composition, shots per turn, who shoots first, and may ships touch?",
      "route": "default"
    },
    {
      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds",
      "category": "ux",
      "changes": "Whether a placement phase, a placement API and drag/rotate UI are built, plus the page structure and the UI test surface.",
      "default": "The server places both fleets randomly when a game starts, and a New game button deals a fresh game. There is no manual placement. The page shows two 10x10 grids: the player's own fleet with incoming shots, and enemy waters where each cell is a real <button> that can be clicked or tapped. A status line reports hit, miss, sunk <ship>, you win and you lose. There is no sound or animation, and the layout is simple and responsive. This rules out manual placement, drag and drop, ship rotation, themes and sound.",
      "id": "Q2",
      "question": "Does the player place their own ships, or is the fleet random? What does the minimal UI have to show?",
      "route": "default"
    },
    {
      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds",
      "category": "requirements",
      "changes": "The AI module design and its tests: invariants versus exact-move assertions, and whether an injectable seeded RNG is needed.",
      "default": "Hunt/target AI. It fires at random unshot cells until a hit, then probes orthogonal neighbours and follows the line until the ship is sunk. It never repeats a shot. It never reads the player's fleet layout and sees only shot outcomes. The RNG is injectable and seedable so tests are deterministic. There is a single difficulty. This rules out difficulty levels, probability-density or learning AIs, and an AI that cheats.",
      "id": "Q3",
      "question": "How strong should the computer opponent be, and must it play fairly?",
      "route": "default"
    },
    {
      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds",
      "category": "architecture",
      "changes": "The API contract, the client/server split, which module owns the rules, and the integration tests (including a check that responses never leak the computer fleet).",
      "default": "The Node server is authoritative. It holds both fleets and the shot history, validates every move, and plays the computer's reply. The browser only renders and sends the clicked coordinate. JSON over plain HTTP: POST /api/games, POST /api/games/:id/shots, GET /api/games/:id. Responses include the computer's counter-shot. The computer's ship positions are never sent until the game is over, then they are revealed. The server rejects out-of-range, repeated, out-of-turn and post-game shots. This rules out client-only game logic, websockets and server push.",
      "id": "Q4",
      "question": "Where does the game logic and hidden state live: in the Node server (authoritative) or in the browser with Node only serving static files?",
      "route": "default"
    },
    {
      "blocks": "nothing: the default proceeds",
      "category": "state",
      "changes": "Game store design, id generation, expiry/cleanup code, reload behaviour in the client, and the lifecycle tests.",
      "default": "Actors: one human player, identified only by an opaque random game id issued by the server (no accounts, cookies or login), and the computer, which is server-side and has no identity. Nothing is shared across people, devices or sessions. A game lives in server memory keyed by its id. The browser keeps the id in sessionStorage, so a reload resumes the game while the server process is alive. A game ends at win or loss, when a new game replaces it, after an idle expiry (60 minutes), or on server restart. Persistence is in-memory only, so a restart loses all games. This rules out a database, cross-device resume, spectators and multiplayer.",
      "id": "Q5",
      "question": "Who are the actors and how are they identified; is any state shared across people, devices or sessions; how long does a game live and what ends it; does a reload resume the game?",

That means node:http for the server, node:test with node:assert for tests, and vanilla HTML/CSS/JS served statically with no build step or framework. Game and AI logic live in a pure module with no DOM or HTTP. package.json provides `npm start` (default port 3000, PORT env override) and `npm test`. If node:test is unavailable on the installed Node, fall back to a dependency-free assert script. This rules out Express, React, bundlers, TypeScript and a database.",

      "question": "Which Node and npm versions are installed, is the npm registry reachable, and should the server use a framework or only built-ins?",

      "blocks": "Only the claim of browser-level verification in the later verify stage. Implementation and the unit/API tests are not blocked.",

      "changes": "The test plan, how the 'works in the browser' claim is evidenced, and whether a headless-browser test is added.",

Unit tests cover the engine (placement validity, shot resolution, sunk and win detection), AI invariants under a seeded RNG (no repeats, targets neighbours after a hit, finishes a game within 100 shots), and the rejected-move cases. HTTP integration tests start the server on an ephemeral port (0) and play a full game through the API. They also assert that GET / serves the page and that no pre-game-over response contains computer ship positions. Browser E2E is added only if a headless browser is already installed. Otherwise the UI is checked by serving the page, and the gap is recorded as an open item. This rules out a new browser-driver dependency.",
      "id": "Q7",
      "question": "What does 'include tests' have to cover, and can the browser UI be exercised automatically in this environment (is a headless browser already installed)?",
      "route": "inspect"

It is playable at http://localhost:3000 when the user runs `npm start`. There is no deployment, hosting, publishing or remote push: the request grants none. If the run is isolated, files appear in the user's checkout only at the final return. Commit only as the harness delivery mode defines. This rules out a public URL, CI setup and containers.",
      "id": "Q8",
      "question": "Where must the result become usable, does the run have authority beyond writing files into the repository, and is the run isolated from the user's checkout?",
      "route": "inspect"
    }

  "summary": "[S1] Outcome (fact): a small single-player Battleship game that a person plays in a web browser against a computer opponent. 'Small' (fact) bounds scope to one page and one game mode, with no accounts and no multiplayer. The consumer is the requester playing locally and the entry point is a localhost URL served by the Node server (assumption). Rules, placement, AI strength, state authority and hidden information are unspecified, so they go to Q1-Q5, each with a recorded default and none needing a person. [S2] Boundary (fact): the server runtime is Node.js, so no other server language. Tests are a required deliverable, not optional. The framework, dependencies and test depth are unspecified, so they go to Q6 and Q7. Assumption: tests run with one command (`npm test`) with no browser or network required. BOUNDARIES. Repository and run scope: the repository is empty (fact from the exercise), so this is greenfield with no conventions or AGENTS.md to inherit, and only the game and its tests are in scope. The run is unattended (fact), so defaults are recorded as assumptions and nothing is asked of a person. Authority (assumption): the request grants creating the code and running it locally for tests. It does not grant deploy, hosting, publishing, pushing to a remote, paid or external services, or global installs. Risks: scope creep (frameworks, database, multiplayer); leaking the computer fleet to the client (Q4); in-memory games lost on restart (Q5); AI and RNG nondeterminism causing flaky tests unless the RNG is injected (Q3, Q7); port clashes in tests (use port 0); Node version drift (Q6); the browser UI being unverifiable without a headless browser (Q7). INTERACTION AND STATE (from the request, else default). Actors: one human, identified only by an opaque server-issued game id, plus the server-side computer (Q5). Shared state: none across people, devices or sessions; single-player is a fact from S1. Lifetime: until win or loss, a new game, 60 minutes idle, or server restart (Q5). Hidden: the computer's fleet is hidden from the browser until game over, and the AI never sees the player's layout (Q4, Q3). The runtime provides an HTTP server, node:test, and browser DOM and fetch. It provides no auth, session store or persistence, so the in-memory default rules out durability. OPEN QUESTIONS (who answers / what it blocks). Q1 rules, Q2 placement and UI, Q3 AI, Q4 authority, Q5 identity and lifetime: recorded defaults, block nothing. Q6 stack: discovery inspects the installed Node/npm and registry reachability, blocks only the scaffold files, and the default applies if inspection fails. Q7 test depth: discovery inspects for a headless browser, blocks only the browser-level verification claim. Q8 delivery: discovery inspects run isolation and delivery mode, blocks only the final return or commit step. DISCOVERY SOURCE HINTS (leads, not verified facts): the local environment (`node --version`, `npm --version`, registry reachability, any installed Chrome, Chromium or Playwright); the harness run metadata (isolated or in-place, target checkout, return and commit mode); Node.js docs for node:http and node:test; the classic Hasbro/Milton Bradley Battleship rules as the rules reference. Ambiguous terms to resolve this way: 'small', 'the computer', 'tests' (unit vs integration vs E2E), 'in the browser' (local vs hosted). The request names no team, workspace, channel, internal site, private repository or owner, so none is looked up. No sensitive locator is involved and nothing needs recording in KNOWLEDGE/. WHERE AND WHEN VISIBLE. The result must become usable in the repository named by the request's working directory (empty today) as a runnable source tree. The request names the browser game and the Node server but no deployed target, so the grant covers only local source and local run. Visibility is at the final return of the run: if the run is isolated, the user's source checkout stays at its snapshot (empty) until then. After that the game is playable at http://localhost:<port> when the user runs `npm start`, and tests run with `npm test`. No release happens and nothing is publicly visible. This intake stage implements nothing and adds no scope."
